messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nikhil sat at his desk on a Thursday morning, the glow from the dual monitors reflecting off the polished surface of his keyboard. The memory that kept him awake in the night, a fractured shard of a police raid he had watched from his living room in 2015, was neither clear nor coherent. He could not lay out the events in order; the details were blocked before they fully formed, as if his mind had tried to push the image away. Yet the feeling that flooded him—intense, unanchored sorrow—arrived with no accompanying visual. When the sudden hiss of a siren or the muffled sound of a bicycle wheel on pavement cut through the hum of his office, he felt that same surge of emotion wash over him, his chest tightening and his palms sweating. Nikhil’s triggers had become a compass that guided his sense of safety. Whenever he felt an unanticipated surge of happiness or a brief moment of relaxation while debugging code, he would immediately seek out a seat that offered a sense of protection—behind the thick glass of his office, surrounded by the familiar hum of servers. The mere sight of a bicycle cycling by on the street outside his building would set his heart racing, and he would glance repeatedly at the cyclist, watching for any sign of threat. Confrontations at work—an angry colleague insisting on a different coding approach—would pull him into a state of hypervigilance, his mind racing through the possibility that anyone could harm him. Those intense triggers fed his belief that the world was fundamentally dangerous. He began to view every encounter with others as a potential threat; the idea that he could be harmed by strangers or even by the person he loved had become a constant undercurrent. The sense that people could read his hidden pain by merely looking at him, as if the event were etched into his skin, reinforced this shattered worldview. His belief that no one could be trusted had become an unshakeable certainty, and the mere thought of a simple cycling motion or a brief laugh could send him spiraling into fear. In the months that followed, the emotional remnants of that police raid seeped into his daily life. When the office’s fluorescent lights flickered, the memory of gunfire rang in his mind, and he felt an inexplicable sense of dread that left him on edge. The more he tried to recall the details of the incident, the less he could. The memory’s fragmented nature allowed it to jump from one trigger to another; a moment of calm would collapse under the weight of a sudden noise, and a sharp reminder of a potential threat would push the memory further away. His safety-seeking behavior became a loop: the triggers drove him to seek protection; the act of seeking protection amplified his belief that the world was unsafe; that belief, in turn, made any new trigger feel even more terrifying, causing him to avoid even benign situations. The constant watching of his coworkers, the avoidance of open spaces in the office, and the choice of a cramped desk corner all reflected a mind that could not escape its own expectations. The cumulative effect of this cycle was tangible. Nikhil’s work quality slipped; the code he wrote became riddled with bugs he would not have written otherwise. His marriage suffered as well; his spouse sensed his distance, his avoidance of shared spaces, and the constant suspicion that something could happen to him. In a meeting with his manager, he missed a presentation, and the conversation that followed was punctuated by his fear of being perceived as weak or unreliable. Those moments only reinforced his fear of harm and his conviction that people were watching him, further tightening the loop of avoidance and dread. Finally, the day he walked into the clinic, the weight of it all seemed too heavy. Nikhil’s constant state of alertness was draining his life. He had begun to dread even routine tasks at work and feared that a single misstep could trigger an outburst of panic. His greatest hope was to regain control over his thoughts, to untangle the memory and make sense of the triggers that had kept him trapped. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never find a place where he could feel safe without the relentless fear that lurked behind every ordinary interaction.
